FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F001  
SEVERITY: 0.79  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.61  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer._check_feasibility()` does not enforce the documented F2 coverage target implied by `_redundancy_target()`. It only checks `matrix[j].sum() >= 1`, while the class docstring and greedy solver logic treat redundancy/coverage level as a constraint dimension for critical and moderate tasks. As a result, an allocation can be reported “feasible” even when every high-criticality task misses its required multiplicity, provided each task has at least one assignee. This is not just optimization shortfall; it downgrades a stated allocation requirement into an unenforced preference.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Separate minimum coverage from redundancy preference explicitly. Either:  
1. redefine F2 in docs and code as “at least one assignee” and state redundancy is soft; or  
2. add a hard feasibility check `matrix[j].sum() >= _redundancy_target(task)` for tasks where redundancy is intended to be mandatory, with a distinct violation code (e.g. F2b). Propagate that status through `solve()`/caller interfaces rather than warning only.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F002  
SEVERITY: 0.72  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.47  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer.__init__()` builds `_model_idx` and `_task_idx` with dict comprehensions that silently overwrite earlier entries on duplicate `model_id` or `task_id`. The rest of the module assumes IDs are unique keys for role lookup and allocation interpretation. With duplicate IDs, role resolution, allocation lookup, and any consumer using `Allocation` by ID become ambiguous or wrong without any explicit failure. This is a structural integrity issue in the load-balancing area’s primary indexing scheme.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Validate uniqueness of `model_id` and `task_id` in `__init__()` and raise a clear `ValueError` on duplicates. Ideally also validate `role_map` keys against the unique model ID set at construction.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F003  
SEVERITY: 0.69  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.50  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer` never validates that every task demand and model capacity is finite and nonnegative before arithmetic. If a `Task.token_demand`, `ModelSpec.L`, `ModelSpec.c`, or `ModelSpec.tau` is `NaN`/`inf`/negative`, numpy comparisons and aggregates can produce silently nonsensical behavior: feasibility checks may fail to flag overloads (`NaN > limit` is false), objective values can become `NaN`, sorting by load fraction can behave unpredictably, and forced assignments can proceed under invalid capacities. A prior finding covers invalid values in domain types globally, but this area independently lacks defensive validation at its trust boundary.  
PROPOSED_FIX: In `LoadBalancer.__init__()` or a dedicated validator, reject non-finite or negative task demands and reject non-finite capacities/costs/latencies. If upstream validation is intended, assert it here and fail closed with descriptive errors.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F004  
SEVERITY: 0.63  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.44  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer.__init__()` accepts any `role_map` and `_admissibility_mask()` silently defaults missing model IDs to `Role.PAR`. This makes incomplete or mismatched role assignments fail open: if a model was omitted from `role_map` due to upstream state skew, it becomes broadly admissible rather than rejected. In a system where role assignment is a separate area and can go stale or become partial, this default can mask cross-component inconsistency and allow unauthorized dispatch patterns.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Validate that `role_map` contains exactly the active model IDs passed to `LoadBalancer`. If a role is missing or there are extra keys, raise or return an explicit infeasibility status. Only default to `PAR` if that behavior is a documented, intentional protocol rule.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F005  
SEVERITY: 0.58  
FLAW_CLASS: 7  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.36  
DESCRIPTION: `solve()` computes `_admissibility_mask()` twice—once inside `_solve_greedy()` and again afterward for `_check_feasibility()`. For current scale this is small, but it is unnecessary duplicated work in the area’s hot path and also creates avoidable risk if admissibility logic later becomes stateful or parameterized.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Compute admissibility once in `solve()` and pass it into `_solve_greedy()` and `_check_feasibility()`, or cache it per solve invocation.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F006  
SEVERITY: 0.57  
FLAW_CLASS: 6  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.52  
DESCRIPTION: `validate_k1()` is too weak to validate the property it claims. Its docstring states “feasibility = sum b_j <= L1,” but the implementation only checks that every task is assigned to the sole model. If total demand exceeds capacity, the validator still returns `True` as long as assignment occurred. This can falsely certify the K=1 reduction property even when the stated feasibility condition is violated.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Extend `validate_k1()` to check both assignment and aggregate feasibility, e.g. `sum(task.token_demand) <= m.L`, and verify no feasibility violations were emitted.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F007  
SEVERITY: 0.54  
FLAW_CLASS: 6  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.49  
DESCRIPTION: `validate_homogeneous()` is also weaker than its stated claim. The docstring says “equal distribution optimal,” but the implementation only returns the boolean from `_balanced()`. Multiple non-equal allocations can satisfy the variance threshold, especially if `epsilon_bal` is loose. So the validator does not actually test the claimed reduction property, only a weaker approximate balance predicate.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Either rename/document it as checking “approximately balanced distribution” or strengthen the validator to assert near-equal per-model loads under a tight tolerance and inspect the actual allocation matrix/load vector.  
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: LB_R2_F008  
SEVERITY: 0.49  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.40  
DESCRIPTION: [CROSS-COMPONENT — unverified from this scope] `dispatch_check()` and `feasibility_probability()` exist as pre-dispatch safeguards for uncertain capacity, but `LoadBalancer.solve()` and `_solve_greedy()` do not incorporate them at all. If upstream orchestration uses `solve()` as the operative allocator without separately filtering assignments through dispatch feasibility, the “Area 2 extension” is disconnected from actual allocation decisions, and assignments may be produced that the extension would advise blocking.  
PROPOSED_FIX: Integrate probabilistic feasibility into admissibility or scoring during allocation, or make the API contract explicit that `solve()` is deterministic-capacity only and must be composed with external dispatch filtering. Surface any resulting mismatch in returned allocation metadata.  
VERIFIED: FALSE

Definitive stance: these are the additional load-balancing flaws I could verify from this area, with one explicit cross-component integration risk noted as unverified.
